Specialty roasters often get asked: “do you know your growers?”

Other “ethical” roasters say they know their farmers. We don’t know ours at all.

‘Knowing your farmers’ sounds ethical. In smallholder-dominated systems, like in East Africa and South East Asia, it usually means the opposite — you’re buying from the wealthiest, best-connected few, and the poorest never get a look in. We built our program to reach them instead.

Why it works where others don’t

“Ethical” usually means a fair price paid to a few. The poorest are quietly left out.

We constantly measure our own performance to find where it can improve, and work with international researchers to test what genuinely improves lives — published in journals including the Journal of Marketing and World Development.

We haven’t returned in six years — yet our pilot’s quality and inclusivity metrics remain as strong as ever. The capability genuinely transferred. Our aim is to scale this into a global, participant-owned initiative.

When is ethical coffee not ethical?
Most specialty and “relationship” coffee controls quality by contracting a small number of larger, better-connected farms.

It’s cheaper to monitor — but it routes the premium to people already doing okay, while the poorest households are left out. Scientists have a name for it: elite capture.

We took the opposite route: an open, low-barrier system that pays directly for quality, that any smallholder can sell into — with lots as little as 5kg. A trusted quality-assessment method does the work that exclusivity does elsewhere, so the chain stays inclusive as it scales.

There are no lock-in contracts and no side-selling monitoring: growers sell to us lot by lot, so we have to be the best option every single time. Our average lot is just 40 kg — smallholder coffee, not estate coffee. And we run the whole chain ourselves, from buying at the farm gate through export, import and roasting to the cafe — so when we tell you where your coffee came from, nothing is taken on trust.

The cup wins on its own

Intensely sweet, juicy, high-grown washed and natural Arabica.

Sourced from the Bugimotwa Growers around Mt Elgon in Kapchorwa, eastern Uganda — some of the oldest volcanic coffee country in East Africa. Slow ripening at altitude and a unique approach to contracting around ripe picking give our lots their signature sweetness.

Intersection Traders began as a partnership between Dr Daniel Gregg, a research economist working in rural development and agri-food supply chains, and Adam Marley, one of Australia’s leading coffee roasters — research rigour on one side, cup quality on the other.

Sustainability

Ongoing work, not a badge.

We treat sustainability the way we treat ethics — as something you do across the whole chain, and keep improving. Currently: fully recyclable bags (moving to 100% home-recyclable), cafe organic waste composted with small local farms, and less sourcing travel — the program is run by locals, not by visiting westerners. Next on the list: building environmental sustainability payments into the buying program itself, so smallholders earn more for looking after the landscape the coffee grows in.
